newsitem.title: UK: Stocks, bonds fall during Greenspan testimony.
newsitem.headline: Stocks, bonds fall during Greenspan testimony.

text.p: Stock and bond prices fell Tuesday as Wall Street braced for more of Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's Congressional testimony on the economy on Wednesday.
The dollar hit a 34-month high against the German mark on expectations of a U.S. interest rate hike and signs that Germany's central bank would not oppose a stronger dollar.
The Dow Jones industrial average fell 66.20 points, or 0.96 percent, to 6,852.72, with nearly all of the drop coming in the last hour of trading.

But in the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,357 to 1,107 on active volume of 536 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange. The Nasdaq composite index, weighted with high-technology stocks, gained 6.19 points to 1,317.37 on strength among tech issues.

Stocks also were pressured by bonds, where the 30-year Treasury bond fell 14/32, or $4.375 on a $1,000 bond, raising its yield to 6.87 percent from 6.83 percent on Monday. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.

"The stock market looked like it was just searching for direction," said Peggy Farley, chief executive at Amas Securities Inc. "It didn't have anything to make it go up and it had Greenspan to make it go down."

Greenspan, who on Wednesday will complete his semi-annual economic report to Congress, put financial markets in a state of high alert last week with blunt warnings on stock prices and interest rates during the first phase of his testimony.
Many Wall Street analysts viewed Greenspan's comments as an attempt to talk the market lower, and blue-chip stocks have declined with only a brief interruption since his appearance.
But during an unrelated appearance on Tuesday before the House Budget Committee, the central bank chief denied his comments were aimed at affecting the market.
"That's not what I was intending to do," he told the committee, later arguing he was incapable of affecting the fundamental course of the market.
"These are very thick, elaborate, international markets which are driven by decisions of millions of people," Greenspan said. "Nobody can affect them in a fundamental way."
Analysts remained unconvinced, however, noting Greenspan said he was still ready to raise interest rates in a bid to head off inflation.

"There's still some concern about what he plans to do," said Philip Orlando, chief investment officer at Value Line Asset Management. "He set the table last week for some preemptive action on interest rates."

The dollar climbed to 1.7162 marks, its highest level since late April 1994, after Bundesbank Council member Guntram Palm said the dollar's recent advance was an "appropriate" correction from its record low in 1995.
The dollar fetched 1.7137 marks in late New York trading, up from 1.6970 marks late on Monday. It rose to 122.15 Japanese yen from 121.24 yen.
Coffee prices staged an explosive rally as scarce supply propelled the market to its highest level in more than 26 months.

The market came within striking distance of the widely watched $2 a pound mark, with the May contract hitting 199.50 cents a pound before settling 10.40 cents higher at 195.25 cents a pound at the Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange.
Overseas, London's FTSE rose 50.6 points to a record 4,357.7, just beating the previous record set Feb. 19. In Tokyo, the 225-share Nikkei average added 135.65 points or 0.74 percent to 18,564.78.
